# Introduction {#introduction}

We have discussed in past articles the [need for a “centralized patient data repository”](https://medium.com/cancerbot/a-vision-for-centralized-patient-data-repositories-80be97b92dda). That article discusses the high level requirements for such a system. It also points towards an architecture for implementation. It can be summarized as: 

1) Use [OMOP](https://www.ohdsi.org/data-standardization/) as the primary store for information, including the OMOP Oncology and Genomics extensions  
2) Add attributes (columns in the OMOP tables) for things that OMOP didn’t quite get to.   
3) Create a “flattened” denormalized version of the patient information. The flattened version is important for use cases such as clinical trial matching, clinical decision support (choosing standard of care options), building predictive models and ease of analytics. [This article](https://medium.com/cancerbot/towards-a-common-patient-information-schema-a1460a835b2f) describes the detailed requirements for that flat patient\_info table.

In this document we expand beyond those two articles describing a data store to a data and services architecture behind a “personal health record” (PHR)  The PHR should do more than just be a long-term store. It can also help manage frequent provider Electronic Health Record imports (FHIR), transform the data into the OMOP form, help patients pick the “source of truth” among conflicting and duplicate health attributes, and provide researchers with the ability to provide analytics on aggregated patient information easier. 

Note that services such clinical decision support, twin matching, and trial matching are not discussed here, but the architecture described supports those add-on capabilities. In the diagram below we list all the  major enabling components of the PHR and the rest of the document describes their details.

![][image1]

Now let’s go through each of these major component layers individually. 

# Extract, Transform and Load {#extract,-transform-and-load}

The PHR architecture includes an ETL layer to manage all of the EHR data sources (via FHIR, custom data formats and PDF scanning).  PHR uses many OHDSI ecosystem components.  But it also adds many components that OHDSI does not attempt to address. First let’s describe what OHDSI out of the box components are used. 

## Core ETL Design & Mapping {#core-etl-design-&-mapping}

**WhiteRabbit** is used to scan source data and produces frequency/profiling reports. **Rabbit-In-A-Hat** is used to map source tables map source tables to OMOP tables, define transformation logic, document ETL decisions.

## Vocabulary Mapping {#vocabulary-mapping}

**OHDSI Athena** is used to manage the standard vocabulary used in the PHR stack for conditions, drugs, procedures, and measurements). **OHDSI Unagi** is used to map the coding used in the source data systems to the standard vocabulary used for analysis. 

## Data Quality Analysis {#data-quality-analysis}

**Achilles Heel** and the **Data Quality Dashboard** are used to find problems in the transformed data. These problems are then fed back to the PHRogrammer component which modifies the transformation scripts accordingly.

### Achilles Heel {#achilles-heel}

This performs a limited set of built-in rules to quickly determine whether a set of ETL transformations is functioning at a surface level . Heel rules are classified into CDM conformance rules and data characterization rules. It catches things like implausible values, referential integrity issues, low data density in critical fields, and concept mapping failures.

### Data Quality Dashboard {#data-quality-dashboard}

The DQD provides thousands of checks down to the record and attribute level (OMOP tables and fields). The PHR architecture provides several additional DQD rules.  Each record is checked for conformance, completeness and plausibility 

## PHR-Created Components: PHRofile, PHRogram and PHResolution {#phr-created-components:-phrofile,-phrogram-and-phresolution}

There are several key gaps that PHR addresses in these tools:

- Ability to do scans and profiling against the hierarchical, nested data in a FHIR JSON bundle (saving a step for ETL developers).  We call this **PHRofile**   
- Generating ETL code that executes the designed mapping.  We call this component **PHRogram.**  It generates Golang scripts that execute the designed mapping and transformation.  The name PHRogram  is a reference to the OHDSI Rabbit-In-A-Hat documentation saying that a programmer is needed to build the actual ETL execution logic once the mappings and transformations are defined.  Our opinion is that insistence on manual programming in 2026 seems quite an unreasonable assumption. The **PHRogrammer** generated transformation scripts and their destination outputs are versioned.   
- Once data is imported the ETL patient resolution component, referred to as **PHResolution**, flags conflicting or likely erroneous data (measurements, observations. procedures, drug exposures) to be reconciled by the patien

![][image2]

# Comprehensive Transactional and Longitudinal Record {#comprehensive-transactional-and-longitudinal-record}

This is the base OMOP schema we have discussed with all of the extensions and additional columns added. The most important tables for the initial scenarios of clinical decision support and trial matching are `condition_occurrence` (cancer diagnoses), `drug_exposure` (prior treatments), `measurement` (biomarkers, labs), `procedure_occurrence`, and `observation_period` (for eligibility window logic). 

The OMOP Oncology and Genomics extensions are added. Lines of Therapy are represented in the OMOP recommended way with the episode and episode\_event tables. Additional columns are added to reflect metadata that OMOP didn’t quite get to. These include richer descriptions of lines of therapy, richer metadata on genomics information (such as assays).  It also includes a new model called PersonLanguageSkill that provides a richer description of patient language capabilities that is necessary for most trials.  

Using OMOP as the base data layer for reflecting the full patient history enables a rich ecosystem of analytics tools and reports, data quality checking suites, and even tools to infer lines of therapy from individual drugs and procedures. OMOP is missing some things to be the true comprehensive long term store of everything you might want for a patient. But we have added those missing columns and models. We have even validated with the OMOP architects that the items that we identified as missing are not in fact present or about to be added. 

![][image3]

# Flattened Patient Information Table  {#flattened-patient-information-table}

`PatientInfo` is explicitly described as a **denormalized integration model** — not an OMOP extension — that aggregates data from standard OMOP tables to support fast clinical trial eligibility screening and AI/ML use cases that won't work natively against OMOP's highly normalized schema. [github](https://github.com/cancerbot-org/ctomop)

It lives in `omop_core` alongside the standard OMOP tables and is populated via a management command (`populate_patient_info`) that extracts and flattens data from across the CDM.

The model has 100+ fields covering demographics and anthropometrics, disease staging and histology, treatment history across all lines, biomarker results (ER, PR, HER2, PD-L1, genetic mutations), laboratory values with units, performance status assessments, social determinants and risk factors, and geographic and language information. [github](https://github.com/cancerbot-org/ctomop)

Key field groupings:

* **Demographics** — sourced from `Person`  
* **Staging** — flattened from `Observation` (TNM, stage group, histology via ICD-O-3)  
* **Treatment lines** — derived from `DrugExposure` patterns, with 1L/2L/later logic, platinum-based and immunotherapy flags  
* **Biomarkers** — pulled from `Measurement` (LOINC-mapped ER, PR, HER2, PD-L1, BRCA1/2, EGFR, KRAS, etc.)  
* **Labs** — hemoglobin, creatinine, LFTs, calcium, albumin, all with units  
* **Social & behavioral** — tobacco status, employment, insurance from `Observation`  
* **Computed fields** — BMI auto-calculated from height/weight measurements

OMOP is normalized for accuracy and interoperability — but that's exactly what makes it slow and awkward for real-time matching. Here's what `PatientInfo` adds:

**1\. Single-table query performance.** Trial matching requires joining 6–8 OMOP tables (Person → ConditionOccurrence → Observation → Measurement × many rows → DrugExposure → Episode…). `PatientInfo` collapses that into one row per patient, making eligibility screening fast enough for real-time use.

**2\. Derived/computed fields OMOP doesn't store.** OMOP records raw drug exposures but doesn't compute treatment lines — `PatientInfo` derives 1L/2L/later from drug exposure patterns and dates, which is essential for matching trials that require "≥2 prior lines."

**3\. AI/ML-ready flat structure.** The README explicitly calls out that the highly normalized OMOP schema "will not work natively" for AI/ML uses — `PatientInfo` provides the flat, feature-vector-like structure that models and matching algorithms need. [github](https://github.com/cancerbot-org/ctomop)

**4\. Snapshot semantics.** Rather than recomputing patient state on every query, `PatientInfo` provides a computed snapshot that can be versioned and audited — important for trial eligibility decisions.

**5\. OMOP compliance is preserved.** All data still lives in standard OMOP tables — `PatientInfo` does not store additional clinical data beyond what's in OMOP, it's purely a performance and usability layer. [github](https://github.com/cancerbot-org/ctomop) This means you get interoperability with OMOP analytics tools AND fast matching.

## Automated Predictive Model Building and Standard of Care Ranking {#automated-predictive-model-building-and-standard-of-care-ranking}

With this “feature vector” available from the flat table, PHR can support generating predictive models of outcomes for any disease and patient cohort that the researcher chooses. A selection of models are generated automatically and kept trained and current for common conditions. These can be used to rank standard of care options for individual patients by performing inference against those

# Analytics Layer {#analytics-layer}

By building on the OMOP CDM standard we get a large amount of analytics capabilities with the [OHDSI Achilles](https://github.com/OHDSI/Achilles) component. 

## Achilles {#achilles}

Achilles is a platform that enables the characterization, quality assessment, and visualization of observational health databases.It's an R package that runs against any OMOP CDM-compliant database and executes over 250 descriptive analyses to produce a comprehensive statistical profile of the data.

---

### Core Analytics Capabilities {#core-analytics-capabilities}

**Database characterization.** Achilles provides an interactive, exploratory framework to assess patient demographics, the prevalence of conditions, drugs and procedures, and to evaluate the distribution of values for clinical observations. [Ohdsi](https://www.ohdsi.org/web/wiki/doku.php?id=documentation:software:achilles)

**Domain-level summaries.** Achilles runs analyses across every major OMOP domain — conditions, drugs, procedures, measurements, observations, visits, and device exposures — generating counts, distributions, and prevalence statistics for each concept in the vocabulary.

**Temporal analysis.** It tracks how data density and concept prevalence change over time, which is critical for understanding data coverage windows and whether a dataset can support longitudinal research.

**Cost analyses.** Achilles can optionally run analyses on COST tables, conditional on CDM version — using older cost tables for CDM v5.0 or the unified cost table for later versions. [OHDSI](https://ohdsi.github.io/Achilles/articles/RunningAchilles.html)

---

### Visualization & Integration {#visualization-&-integration}

Achilles results feed into two main UIs:

* **ATLAS Data Sources** — the primary dashboard for browsing Achilles results, showing treemaps, histograms, and concept-level drilldowns across all domains  
* **ARES** — a newer RShiny-based viewer focused on data quality and longitudinal data source monitoring (the successor to the now-deprecated AchillesWeb)

## Custom Analytics {#custom-analytics}

The Personal Health Record provides several metrics that are not provided by Achilles or the OHDSI ecosystem. There are many out of the box analytics that PHR adds that drastically accelerate medical informaticians work in both outcome analysis and characterizing datasets. 

![][image5]

### 📈 Outcome Analysis  {#📈-outcome-analysis}

When analyzing treatments there are a set of standard metrics that are expected to be provided. The OHDSI ecosystem does not provide any out of the box for these metrics. We can save analysts and informaticians a large amount of work by providing them.  For lines of therapy and other treatments (i.e. can be for adjuvant or neo-adjuvant therapies) the PHR data architecture provides the following metrics:

- Overall Response Rate   
- Complete Response  
- Partial Response  
- Median Duration of Response  
- Median Progression-Free Survival  
- Median Overall Survival  
- Cytokine Release Syndrome (any grade and \>=3)  
- ICANS (any grade and \>=3)

The following dimensions can be used to provide more insights into these metrics:

- disease, disease sub-type  
- adjuvant therapy, neo-adjuvant therapy   
- whether or not progression was observed

### 📊 Primary Data Characterization Metrics {#📊-primary-data-characterization-metrics}

| Metric  | What It Counts | Dimensions |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| patient\_count | Distinct patients | Gender, race, ethnicity, age group, birth year; filterable to myeloma-only  |
| condition\_prevalence | Distinct patients per condition | Condition name, start year, gender, age group  |
| drug\_exposure\_count | Drug exposure events \+ distinct patients | Drug name, start year, gender; pre-built filters for lenalidomide, bortezomib, dexamethasone |

### 🏥 Data Characterization Detail  {#🏥-data-characterization-detail}

| Model | What it computes |
| ----- | ----- |
| `dq__source_summary` | Row counts, person counts, records-per-person for every OMOP domain table |
| `dq__person_summary` | Gender / race / ethnicity / birth year distributions with % of total |
| `dq__observation_period_summary` | Length quantiles (P10–P90), persons by enrollment start year, periods-per-person distribution |
| `dq__domain_concept_summary` | Per-concept person \+ record counts across conditions, drugs, measurements, observations, procedures, drug\_era, condition\_era |
| `dq__concept_demographics` | Per-concept breakdown by 10-year age bucket and gender (concepts with ≥10 persons) |
| `dq__concept_temporal` | Monthly prevalence per 1,000 active persons for top concepts per domain |
| `dq__data_density` | Records per domain per month — data completeness over time |
| `dq__concept_violations` | Unmapped rate, source-concept completeness, domain conformance per concept (OHDSI DQD checks) |
| `dq__death_summary` | Deaths by cause concept, age-at-death bucket, and year |
| `dq__location_summary` | Patient count by city/state (small-cell suppressed: \<5 excluded) |

### 🧬 Disease-specific core models  {#🧬-disease-specific-core-models}

| Model | What it provides |
| ----- | ----- |
| `core__lines_of_therapy_validated` | One row per AI-validated LoT: line number, drug regimen (all/induction/maintenance phases), procedures, CAR-T & transplant flags, bispecific flag, clinical trial linkage, PFS inputs (progression date, censoring date), user demographics |
| `core__genetics` | Wide pivot of cytogenetic test results per user — deletions, gains, amplifications, duplications, translocations, trisomies, monosomies across \~60 canonical loci |
| `core__survey_responses` | One row per user × survey × question — full PRO/survey answer OBT |

# Conclusion {#conclusion}

The data and backend services architecture described here enables a new kind of product to help patients that we refer to as a Personal Health Record.. PHRs enable patients to truly own the truth of the full health picture. The PHR acts as a solid foundation to let other patient services, from clinical decision support to twin matching, to electronic doctor-patient collaboration, to clinical trial matching work optimally for better patient outcomes.
